ImgSearch · independent allocation study · 10 September 2026

The 10M Corpus Allocation

Built from scratch: live demand data, live Commons and Openverse API measurements, a SigLIP relevance experiment, and a look at what the running 435k corpus actually returns for the queries our users type. Six of the findings below contradict the two allocation documents already in this folder. Every number here is either a live API response taken today, a measurement I ran, or a file reference — nothing is inherited.

147,450,017files on Commons today — meta=siteinfo, live
56%of a real Commons harvest is share-alike, which the app hides by default
~48MCommons bitmaps in commercially clean licence categories — 4.8× the target
800–1,200search topics needed to reach 10M. That, not the bucket table, is the deliverable

1 · Six findings that change the plan

Each of these is a measurement, not an opinion. Each one moves the plan somewhere the existing documents do not go.

1. Relevance search beats category traversal, and it is not close

Both prior plans build the corpus by walking Commons category trees recursively. I compared that against harvesting by generator=search in relevance order, on the same topic, by eye. The ten-thousandth result of the search harvest is better than the fiftieth file of the category walk. Category order is a sort key, not a ranking: there is no way to take the best n from a category, because a category has no best.

Evidence: §4, two contact sheets.

2. 56% of Commons is share-alike, and the app hides it by default

SearchView.swift:12 sets hideShareAlike = true. In a 1,400-file sample of a real harvest, 56% of files carried a CC-BY-SA licence. A Commons-only 10M build as specified would therefore ship 4.4M images a default user can see, not 10M. But Commons exposes licence as a flat category, and incategory:"CC-Zero" works inside search — so the whole crawl can be licence-sharded at source, and there are ~48M commercially clean bitmaps to draw from.

Evidence: §6.

3. The best results in the live corpus are not from Commons

I queried the running 435k index for the fourteen things creators actually search, then checked the provenance of what came back. The three rows that look best — concrete texture, smoke on black, bokeh — are 80% Openverse. The two rows that look worst are 100% Commons. A Commons-only 10M build is a regression in exactly the categories editors reach for most.

Evidence: §7, §8.

4. Per-topic yield varies 20-fold and cannot be predicted from category size

I embedded harvested images with the project's own SigLIP model and scored them against the topic. sunset holds its relevance flat to rank 9,950. coffee — a comparable 77,736 hits — collapses by rank 1,500 into photographs of shopfronts with "coffee" in the name. You cannot decide that a bucket will contain 2.4M images. You can only measure where each topic runs out.

Evidence: §5.

5. Search harvesting fixes the metadata problem that enumeration created

docs/10m-plan.html lists a retrieval caveat: enumeration yields files named Ph-1.jpg with no text, so the BM25 half of hybrid retrieval starves. In my harvest sample, 97% of rows carried a description — necessarily, because search selects on text. The mechanism that improves picture quality also repairs the lexical index. That is not a trade-off, it is the same decision paying twice.

Evidence: §9.

6. The binding constraint is the topic list, and the repo already said so

imgsearch-proto/README.md:271-274: "images ≈ topics × sources × per_topic × fill_rate … To reach 300k you need ~500 topics, not more machines. Expand seeds.txt first." That law was written for the prototype and then forgotten by both allocation documents, which reason in millions per bucket. Measured across 56 real topics, the clean-licence addressable pool is 2,465,274 — a median of 52,570 per topic. After the relevance gate and cross-topic dedup, 10M needs roughly 800–1,200 topics. seeds.txt has 481.

Evidence: §12.

2 · Who this is for, and what fails them today

Not "creatives". Six jobs, each with a different failure mode. I ran fourteen queries drawn from these jobs against the live 435k index and looked at the top eight for each.

JobWhat they typeWhat they need it to doStatus at 435k
Faceless / explainer / documentary YouTubevaranasi ghats, kaaba, earth from space, steam locomotive, medieval manuscriptContext B-roll under a voiceover. Needs breadth of subject far more than gloss.strong
Client video editors & motion designerssmoke on black, bokeh light leak, storm clouds, water splash, aerial drone cityPlates and overlays to composite. Needs clean backgrounds, not documentation.strong — via Openverse
Design / editorial / collagevintage travel poster, ukiyo-e, botanical plate, patent drawing, art decoPublic-domain source material nobody else indexes. The differentiator.excellent
Indian & Muslim creatorsganesh murti, shiv ji, durga puja, varanasi, kaaba, madina, masjid nabawi, onamCulturally specific imagery that Western stock libraries barely stock.present, shallow
Thumbnail makers (YouTube / Instagram)faces with strong emotion, product lineups, single object on blackPunch at 168px. Faces drive +20–30% CTR.weak, and unfixable
Office / teachers / Canvaoffice workers meeting, business people, isolated object on white, clean diagramModern corporate stock. Model-released, generic, clean.weak

The two red rows are the same problem and it is not a corpus problem. Expressive modern faces and clean product cutouts barely exist under a free licence anywhere, because both require a release or a studio. Chasing them with more crawling wastes the build. The thumbnail job is still winnable — but through the other half of a thumbnail: the background, the object, the plate. Serve that, and let the creator supply their own face.

Thumbnails — what the CTR research actually says

Faces carrying strong emotion raise click-through by 20–30%; videos with human faces in the thumbnail take substantially more views; thumbnails with more than three distinct elements lose about 23% of their CTR, and fewer than four words of text gains about 30%. Every one of those findings points at material we cannot supply and must not pretend to: released, expressive, modern faces.

What the same research also says, and what we can supply: high contrast, a single dominant subject at 40–60% of frame, and simple backgrounds. That is a plate-and-object job, and it is the half of the thumbnail brief we should own.

What demand looks like once you stop counting keywords

Sorting every list above by what the image is for rather than what it depicts collapses to four classes:

  1. Establishing and context — landscape, city, landmark, weather, aerial. Largest by volume everywhere.
  2. Surface and atmosphere — wallpaper, background, texture, abstract, bokeh, smoke. Two of Pexels' evergreen top three.
  3. Named subject — dog, cat, flower, coffee, car, mosque, ganesh murti. Long tail, high intent, easy to satisfy or fail obviously.
  4. People doing things — person, couple, doctor, office, discussion. High volume, lowest free-licence supply.

The allocation in §11 is organised on these four, not on a subject taxonomy, because the four have genuinely different supply economics and genuinely different failure modes.

4 · Supply: how you enumerate matters more than what you enumerate

Commons, live today

Resolution is not a constraint anywhere. 83M files clear a 2000px bar, and we display at 384px. Nothing in this plan should ever be sized by "are there enough big images" — there are.

Four ways to enumerate, and only one of them is good

MechanismDepth per queryOrderMetadataVerdict
generator=allimageswhat built the 24k enumerated sampleunboundedfilenameoften noneworst
generator=categorymemberswhat both prior plans proposeunboundedsort keyvariesmediocre
generator=searchrelevance harvest, licence-sharded10,000 hard caprelevance97% have textwinner

Structured data is the tempting one and it dies on volume: P180=Q144 (depicts dog) returns 26,096 files, Q146 (cat) 40,755, Q8502 (mountain) 31,895, Q61509 (sunset) 1,106. Against a 10M target that is a rounding error. Revisit in two years.

The search cap is real and exact: sroffset=9990 returns results, sroffset=10500 returns "Up to 10000 search results are supported". That cap turns out not to matter, for the reason in §5 — almost no topic stays relevant that deep — and where it does matter, licence sharding multiplies it, because each licence category is a separate query with its own 10,000.

A tool that looks like the answer and is not. Commons search supports deepcat:"X", which resolves a category tree in one request. It warns "Deep category query returned too many categories. Only a subset has been applied" on almost every real root, and it is not even self-consistent: deepcat:"Butterflies" returned 61 files, while the same query intersected with Quality images returned 2,667 — a subset larger than its superset. Do not size a bucket with deepcat. I nearly did.

The comparison, by eye

Both prior documents build the corpus from the second image. That is the single largest quality decision in the plan and neither of them tested it.

5 · The relevance-decay experiment

The measurement that turns the allocation table from a wish into a budget.

Method: for eight topics, harvest sixteen images at each of seven ranks, embed them with the project's own ViT-B-16-SigLIP / webli on MPS, and score each against "a photo of {topic}" using the model's own sigmoid calibration — sigmoid(117.33·cos − 12.93), the same scale and bias safety.py uses. Median over sixteen. This is not a proxy for quality: it is the exact number the crawler can compute for free at ingest, because the vector is already in memory.

Topicbitmap hits05001,5003,0005,0007,5009,950Usable depth
sunset282,520.047.127.204.093.133.092.11810,000+
cat21,959,836.210.080.062.067.043.092.12310,000+
autumn forest17,015.527.167.041.196.066.323.022~7,500
mountain landscape74,070.030.023.023.028.014.000.005~5,000
coffee77,736.049.051.008.004.002.004.000~1,000
smoke83,948.001.003.010.000.008.001.000~0
concrete wall texture669.002.000—————~0
office workers meeting491.008——————~0

Three things fall out of this table and each one is load-bearing.

a. Hit count does not predict usable depth

coffee and mountain landscape have almost the same hit count — 77,736 against 74,070 — and differ five-fold in usable depth. smoke has 83,948 hits and essentially zero usable depth, because the word matches smokestacks, smoking, and tobacco packaging, not the plate an editor wants. cat reports 21,959,836 hits, which is nonsense produced by term ambiguity, and still harvests cleanly because relevance ranking sorts the nonsense to the back.

b. Therefore a bucket target is a budget, not a quota

"Nature and landscape: 2,400,000" is not something you can decide. It is the sum of a few hundred topics' individual, unpredictable, measured-at-runtime yields. Both prior tables present these numbers as targets; they are better read as spending caps and priority order.

c. The stopping rule should be the score, not a rank

Crawl a topic in relevance order and stop when the running median SigLIP score against that topic falls below a floor for k consecutive batches. That costs one dot product per image against a vector we already have, needs no second model, and is the mechanism §13 specifies. It replaces the fixed keep/drop prompt list in corpus_plan.json, which asks a generic question ("is this a photograph?") when the useful question is specific ("is this the thing I searched for?").

A useful accident. The relevance gate subsumes most of what the quality gate was for. A scanned book page harvested under "sunset" scores near zero against "a photo of sunset" and is dropped without anyone needing to write a prompt for book pages. Keep a short generic drop list for the things that score well and are still useless — heraldic shields, herbarium sheets, screenshots — but the bulk of the filtering is free.

6 · Licences: the lever nobody pulled

I sampled 1,400 files from a real relevance harvest across ten topics and three depths, and read the licence off extmetadata:

LicenceCountShareDefault visibility in the app
CC BY-SA (4.0, 3.0, 2.5, 2.0 and variants)78456.0%hidden
Public domain24217.3%shown
CC BY (4.0, 3.0, 2.5, 2.0)25017.9%shown
CC0997.1%shown
GFDL, FAL, other251.8%excluded

Crawled naively, a 10M Commons corpus is a 4.4M corpus for a default user. SearchView.swift:12 sets hideShareAlike = true and there is no UI to turn it off (imgsearch-mac/README.md, "Not built yet"). Neither prior allocation mentions this. It halves everything both of them propose.

The fix is one search operator

Commons records licence as a flat maintenance category, and incategory: composes with everything else in search. Verified live today, restricted to bitmaps:

Licence categoryBitmaps via searchFiles via categoryinfoSubcatsCommercial use
CC-PD-Mark13,800,72716,984,2740clean
CC-Zero8,391,4879,799,04913clean
CC-BY-2.07,861,700——clean
CC-BY-4.06,485,3768,396,7492clean
PD-old-100-expired6,455,7877,770,78921clean
CC-BY-3.03,092,344——clean
PD-self1,467,910——clean
PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)836,234——clean
PD-1996314,505——clean
CC-BY-SA-4.031,982,615——hidden by default

Allowing for overlap between the PD tags, that is on the order of ~48M gross / realistically 35–40M unique commercially clean bitmaps — three to four times the target. A 10M corpus with zero share-alike in it is comfortably available.

Three consequences

  1. Every crawled image counts. No image is fetched, embedded and indexed only to be hidden from the default user. That is the single biggest efficiency gain in this document — worth more than any bucket reweighting.
  2. The 10,000-result cap effectively multiplies by eight. Licence shards are disjoint, so sunset incategory:"CC-Zero" and sunset incategory:"CC-BY-2.0" are separate queries with separate caps. Measured for sunset: 55,403 addressable across eight shards versus a 10,000 ceiling unsharded.
  3. It changes the quality distribution, so it needs the gate. CC0 on Commons skews toward Wikimedia-event and institutional uploads: sunset incategory:"CC-Zero" is beautiful at rank 0–15 and by rank 2,000 has drifted into conference photographs and group selfies. The relevance gate catches this; a fixed depth would not.

One syntax note, verified: incategory:"A"|"B" returns zero. There is no OR form. Run one query per licence category — which, per point 2, you want anyway.

7 · Where Commons genuinely fails

Three independent instruments, all pointing at the same two holes.

TopicAll bitmapsClean-licence addressableSigLIP @ rank 0Verdict

texture113,89133,096—building materials, not plates
man working7,7873,866—documentary only
portrait woman45,54030,401—historical skew

Commons does not shoot surfaces, and it does not shoot modern working life. Both are structural, not incidental: Commons is an encyclopaedic archive of things that exist, and a seamless concrete texture is not a thing that exists, it is a photograph made for compositing. No amount of category traversal, licence sharding or extra crawl hours changes this. Both prior documents mark these buckets WEAK and then allocate 350,000–1,200,000 images to them from Commons anyway.

But the running corpus already serves them well — from somewhere else

The contact sheet in §2 shows concrete texture, smoke-on-black and bokeh as three of the strongest rows in the whole grid. I checked where those results come from by reading the id prefix on the live API response:

This is the finding that most changes the plan. The current corpus is only 435k and it already beats a hypothetical Commons-only 10M for editors, because 14% of it comes from somewhere Commons cannot reach. Dropping Openverse to simplify the architecture would make the product worse while making the number bigger.

8 · The other 800 million images

Openverse's own stats endpoint, live today — 52 providers, 915,519,784 works:

ProviderWorksWhat it is worth to us
Flickr536,219,600The plate and texture library. Where our best surfaces already come from. Own CDN, own sizes.
iNaturalist266,268,617Field-observation biology. Enormous and almost entirely unusable — this is the biology trap at its purest.
Wikimedia Commons88,962,441Already covered directly, at greater depth, without Openverse's cap.
Europeana13,841,364European archives. Treasury material.
Smithsonian NMNH4,990,743Specimen-heavy; select, do not sweep.
Rawpixel1,268,095Highest value per image in the whole list. CC0 vintage posters, botanical plates, paper textures, patterns — exactly our two weak buckets, made for design use.
Geograph Britain and Ireland1,090,119Systematic UK landscape. Good establishing-shot depth.
Metropolitan Museum of Art498,428Treasury. Also reachable directly (below).
NASA131,756Space and earth. Public domain by statute.

Openverse is capped at 240 results per query for anonymous callers — verbatim from the API: "pagination depth may not exceed 240 for anonymous requests". Page 12 returns results; page 13 returns that error. So Openverse is a discovery layer, not a bulk source, exactly as imgsearch-proto/README.md says. At 240 per query, a million images needs ~4,200 distinct queries before overlap.

Two things I verified that change the cost model

Non-Commons sources do not need a bucket either

redundant documents/superseded-corpus-plans/final-report.html concludes "B2 only for non-Commons origins". I do not think that holds. Openverse returns Flickr originals as live.staticflickr.com/…_b.jpg, and Flickr's size suffixes are a pure string substitution. Fetched live:

SuffixNominal sizeBytesHTTP
_b1024px223,082200
_c800px159,467200
_z640px103,910200
_n320px25,825200
_m240px14,790200

25.8 KB at 320px is within 22% of the 21.2 KB mean measured for Commons 384px WebP in TEST-DRIVE.md Step A. The Met is the same story — primaryImageSmall on object 45734 hotlinks at HTTP 200, 38,711 bytes, image/jpeg, from images.metmuseum.org. Store thumb_origin for these sources too and the build still needs no bucket, no egress allowance and no card. That deletes the last argument for reintroducing B2.

The direct route beats the Openverse route where it exists

Openverse's 240-cap applies to Openverse, not to the providers. Flickr's own API takes a free key with no card, filters by CC licence, and shards by upload-date window for unbounded depth; the Met's collection API is open, unauthenticated, and reports 502,708 objects. For the two buckets Commons cannot fill, go to the source; use Openverse for discovery and for the long tail of the other 45 providers.

9 · Keep rate, measured end to end

redundant documents/superseded-corpus-plans/final-report.html assumes "~30% quality/safety/dedup/licence loss" and Gemini's review correctly flags that the figure appears nowhere in the test drive. Here it is, measured on 1,400 files from a real harvest across ten topics and three depths:

FilterPassingRateNote
Licence is PD / CC0 / CC-BY, no ND, no NC1,38398.8%Rises to ~100% once the crawl is licence-sharded
≥ 640 × 4801,29692.6%The real cost. Small historical scans
Aspect ratio ≤ 3:11,38999.2%Panoramas and scroll scans
API returned a thumb_origin1,400100%Serving is never the blocker
Carries a description (feeds BM25)1,35897.0%vs. near-zero for flat enumeration
All metadata filters together1,26990.6%Before download

Those filters run off the API row, before any image is fetched. The post-download losses are known from the test drive: safety at threshold 0.005 removes ~0.4%; near-duplicates sit at 11.5% within cosine 0.95, of which perhaps 6–8% is worth dropping. The relevance gate is the unknown — call it 20–25% until the pilot measures it, since removing the tail is the whole point.

rows returned by search      14.9M
  × 0.92  metadata filters  13.7M   ← downloaded and embedded
  × 0.996 safety            13.6M
  × 0.78  relevance gate    10.6M
  × 0.94  near-dup cap      10.0M   ← indexed, 100% default-visible

At the measured coupled rate of 4.6 img/s per runner, 13.7M downloads across 40 Pro-tier runners is ≈ 21 hours of crawl, or roughly four to six re-runs against the 6-hour job ceiling. That sits inside the 26–30 h band imgsearch-proto/README.md already projects, and the 3.7M images discarded after download are the price of the quality the gate buys.

10 · Where I disagree with the two prior documents

redundant documents/superseded-corpus-plans/corpus-plan.html and redundant documents/superseded-corpus-plans/final-report.html are mine; redundant documents/superseded-corpus-plans/final-report-reviewed.html is Gemini's review. I read all three, tested their claims, and kept what survived.

Disagreements

1 · Both build on category traversal. It is the wrong mechanism.

corpus_plan.json lists 13 buckets of Commons category roots and notes "every root below is walked recursively". final-report.html §9 calls recursive traversal "half a day, only real code". Gemini's Gap 4 correctly flags that traversal is untested — but then accepts it as the plan. I tested it against relevance search on the same topic and it loses badly (§4). Category traversal should be kept only as the fallback for topics with no useful text, which after licence sharding is a small set.

2 · Neither noticed that the corpus would be 56% invisible.

Nothing in either document mentions share-alike composition. The app hides it by default and has no toggle. This is a 2× error on every number in both tables, and it is fixable with one search operator (§6).

3 · "Commons-only, store nothing" is right about storage and wrong about sources.

final-report.html concludes "Serving stays $0 Wikimedia CDN. No B2 unless multi-source returns," and treats multi-source as a cost event. But the best-performing rows in the live index are already 80% Openverse (§7), and Flickr and the Met serve their own sized derivatives that hotlink at HTTP 200 (§8). Multi-source and no-bucket are not in tension. The prototype's own architecture already did this; the 10M plan quietly dropped it and called the result a simplification.

4 · The "textures are weak" diagnosis was right for the wrong reason, and the prescription was wrong.

corpus_plan.json justifies a 350k texture bucket with "WEAK on Commons, which does not shoot for this use". Gemini disagrees and proposes 500–800k via Architectural textures, Paper, Marbled paper, Macro. I measured it three ways — search counts, SigLIP relevance, and a contact sheet that ran dry at sixteen images — and Commons cannot fill either figure. Gemini is right that the roots matter and wrong that better roots solve it. The answer is source, not roots: Flickr and Rawpixel, at a smaller number (§11, Class F).

5 · Both present bucket sizes as targets. They are budgets.

Gemini's table hits 10,000,000 exactly and assumes 100% fill; mine came to 13.7M gross with a hand-waved 30% attrition. Both are fiction in the same way: per-topic yield varies twenty-fold and is not predictable from any number you can look up (§5). The honest artefact is a priority-ordered topic list with a measured stopping rule, and a table that says "spend no more than this here".

6 · The quality gate asks the wrong question.

corpus_plan.json's gate scores every image against generic prompts — "a photograph" versus "a scanned page of a book". Useful, but weak: it cannot tell a beautiful photograph of a car park from a beautiful photograph of a sunset when you asked for a sunset. Scoring against the topic that retrieved the image is strictly more informative, costs the same matmul, and drops book pages for free (§13).

11 · The allocation

10,000,000 net, indexed, and 100% visible to a default user. Organised by the job the image does, because that is what determines both supply economics and failure mode. Every figure is a ceiling and a priority, not a promise.

Class / bucketNet targetShareWhy this size
A · Establishing & contextthe largest job, and Commons' one true superpower3,400,00034%Unsplash landscape is 11,049,027 searches, 2.4× the next category; Pexels evergreen carries landscape, beach, mountain, sunset. Commons is organised geographically and holds 101M bitmaps over 1500px. This is the one place where demand rank and supply rank agree.
Natural landscape & wildernesssunset · mountain · forest · desert · coast · waterfall · lake · glacier · canyon · seasons1,300,000Deepest measured topics: sunset holds relevance to 10,000, waterfall 65,207 addressable clean.
Cities, streets, architecture, interiorsskyline · street · bridge · castle · temple · station · staircase · door · room1,250,000castle 77,950 · bridge 71,294 · church interior 63,122 addressable clean. Gate hard — Commons architecture skews to documentation.
Landmarks & travel destinationsnamed places, city-by-city, monument-by-monument500,000Pexels country lists are full of place names — hamburg, glasgow, valencia, rio de janeiro, varanasi, paris. Proper nouns are exactly where hybrid BM25 beats dense-only.
Weather, sky, aerialsstorm clouds · fog · rain · snow · aerial · drone view350,000The one plate category Commons can serve — aerial view city 11,948 clean, and the live "aerial drone city" row is already good.
B · Named subjectsthe "I need a picture of X" job2,150,00021.5%High-intent long tail. Easy to satisfy, and obvious when you fail.
Animals & wildlife gatediconic species, action, macro — never a taxonomic sweep550,000Pexels evergreen dog and cat. Cut hard from the prior 1.6M: the tree is deep but mostly specimen photography. Prefer Quality-images members first.
Food & drinkdish · bakery · market · coffee · street food · cuisine by country500,000Unsplash food is 4,552,145 searches. food dish 65,387 clean addressable. But coffee dies at rank ~1,000 — needs many narrow topics, not few broad ones.
Plants & flowers gatedflower · rose · tree · garden · leaf · autumn colour400,000Pexels evergreen #3. Same herbarium trap as animals; flower is 70,480 clean addressable, mostly fine, but the tail is specimen sheets.
Transport & machinescar · train · aircraft · ship · bicycle · engine · industrial400,000super car and bmw appear on the India and Türkiye lists; steam locomotive is already one of the better live rows.
Objects, tools, instrumentson a plain ground where it exists — never a cutout bucket300,000Unsplash "supplies" is 2,357,492 searches. Serve the object; refuse the cutout (§10).
C · Treasury the moat100% public domain — no share-alike, no releases, no takedown exposure2,300,00023%The only class no competitor has at hotkey speed. PD-old-100-expired alone is 7,770,789 files and CC-PD-Mark 16,984,274, so supply is 8× the ask. Pexels tracks black and white at 991K searches; vintage, retro and aesthetic recur on every list. And it is the cheapest class to crawl cleanly, because the licence shard is the topic filter.
Painting, drawing, print, ukiyo-e850,000painting 78,226 clean addressable; Met 498,428 works; Rijksmuseum and Europeana behind that.
Historical & documentary photographyB&W, war, retro technology, street, portraiture by decade700,000Also the only honest way to serve "people" at volume — see Class G.
Posters, advertising, ephemera, patents550,000poster 60,181 clean addressable. Best row in the live grid. Rawpixel adds CC0 depth.
Manuscripts, botanical plates, decorative maps200,000manuscript 66,127 clean addressable. Cap it — this is where near-duplicate microfilm runs live.
D · Culture, religion & festivalshinduism · islam · christianity · buddhism · temples · mosques · churches · festivals · dress · rites900,0009%Highest demand-to-supply-elsewhere ratio measured. madina and masjid nabawi are globally trending on Pexels; makkah, kaaba, islamic, jesus, ganesh murti, shiv ji, durga puja, varanasi, onam recur across five country lists. Commons is deep — temple 68,943 and mosque 48,043 clean addressable — and Unsplash is not. Raised from 550k.
E · Science, space & explainerastronomy · earth observation · anatomy · microscopy · laboratory · engineering550,0005.5%Directly serves the faceless-explainer job. NASA and ESA are public domain by statute. laboratory science 46,522 clean addressable. Cap and dedup aggressively — the live "earth from space" row is eight copies of one photograph.
F · Surfaces & atmosphere plates not Commonsconcrete · wood · paper · fabric · rust · marble · smoke · fire · water · bokeh · grain · gradient500,0005%Demand is top-three on Pexels (wallpaper, background, texture). Commons supply is measured at effectively zero (§7). This bucket comes from Flickr, Rawpixel and Openverse or it does not exist. Highest-risk line in the table and the first thing to pilot. If the pilot returns under 50% fill, cut it to 200k and build background-removal in the app instead.
G · People & daily life documentary onlystreet · crowds · occupations · performers · hands · historical portraiture200,0002%Unsplash "person" is 3,085,639 searches and I am still allocating 2%, deliberately. office workers meeting returns 491 Commons bitmaps; the live results are government press photography. Modern corporate stock does not exist under a free licence and CC never conveys a model release. People arrive incidentally in Classes A, C and D — festivals, markets, streets, archives — which is the honest way to serve the query. Ship a release warning on any image with detected faces before this ships at all.
Total10,000,000≈ 14.9M search rows examined, ≈ 13.7M images downloaded and embedded, ≈ 21 h of crawl on 40 runners.

Quality images is not a bucket. corpus_plan.json allocates 462,000 to "Quality images (flat, vetted)" alongside thirteen subject buckets that would also contain those same files — it double-counts. The 462,631 Quality images, 22,339 Featured pictures and 2,263 Valued images are a layer: crawl them first because they are flat, cheap and pre-vetted, dedupe by page id, and let each one land in whichever class it belongs to. They are about 4.9% of the target and they arrive in roughly an hour.

12 · The topic list is the real artefact

I measured the clean-licence addressable pool for 56 representative topics across eight licence shards, capping each shard at the API's 10,000:

2,465,274addressable across 56 topics
52,570median per topic
104worst topic (bokeh lights)
18 / 56topics below 20,000

Addressable is not usable — the relevance gate and cross-topic dedup take most of it. Extrapolating from the measured distribution, and assuming a usable fraction between a quarter and a half, 10M net needs on the order of 800–1,200 topics. seeds.txt currently holds 481, written for a 25k prototype. So the honest statement of remaining work is not "walk thirteen category trees" — it is "write another five hundred to a thousand good topics, then let the gate decide how deep each one goes."

That is a day of writing, and it is the highest-leverage day in the project. It is also the step where the allocation table above actually gets applied: you write topics until each class has enough of them, and the class targets tell you when to stop.

What makes a good topic, measured

PropertyGoodBadWhy
Visual specificitysunset, autumn forestcoffee, smokeWords that name what a picture looks like stay relevant deep; words that name an industry or substance drift into signage and infrastructure within 1,500 ranks.
Length1–2 words3+ wordsCirrus ANDs terms. concrete wall texture has 669 hits; texture has 113,891. Narrow with a licence shard or a second topic, not with more words.
Ambiguitydistinctive nounscat, street, mapstreet reports 88,544,755 hits and sculpture 121,906,555 — the term is matching boilerplate. Harmless, because relevance still sorts, but never size a bucket from the count.
Overlapdistinct subjectsmodifier cross-productsAlready recorded at seeds.txt:3-4: near-duplicate topics return overlapping results and waste the budget. Dedup by page id across topics regardless.

13 · The relevance gate

One number, computed from a vector that is already in memory, replacing both the fixed harvest depth and most of the quality prompt list.

for each (topic, licence_shard):
    t = encode_text("a photo of " + topic)          # once, cached
    for batch in harvest(topic, shard, offset += 50):
        v = encode_image(batch)                      # already required for indexing
        rel = sigmoid(117.33 * (v @ t) - 12.93)      # same calibration as safety.py

        keep  = rel >= REL_MIN                       # calibrate in the pilot
        keep &= safety(v) < 0.005                    # TEST-DRIVE.md, unchanged
        keep &= generic_drop(v) < DROP_MAX           # short list: heraldry, herbarium,
                                                     # screenshots, catalogue cards
        if median(rel) < REL_MIN for k consecutive batches:
            break                                    # this topic is exhausted

Notes that matter:

  • It costs nothing. One extra column in a matmul the crawler already runs for safety. safety.py's frozen-prompt design (an 86 KB npz, numpy only, no torch) extends to topic vectors unchanged.
  • The threshold is per-topic-relative, not absolute. Absolute SigLIP sigmoid values vary by prompt — autumn forest peaks at .527 while mountain landscape peaks at .030 (§5). Gate on the ratio to the topic's own rank-0 median, not on a global constant.
  • It gives the crawler a stopping rule, which the fixed-quota design never had. imgsearch-proto/README.md records that the 500k run "ended when the slowest quota ended, not when the work did" and prescribes a claim-based queue. A claim queue over topics, with the gate deciding when each topic is finished, is that fix and this fix at once.
  • Calibrate it before trusting it. Same discipline as the safety threshold: harvest one topic to 10,000, score every image, look at 50 images either side of the candidate cut, and pick the value where a human agrees. Do not pick it from a percentile.

The known failure mode. SigLIP scores an image against words, so the gate will systematically prefer images that look like the stereotype of a topic. For "sunset" that is fine. For "varanasi" it may prefer the postcard ghat over the interesting one. Where a class is culturally specific — Class D above all — keep the threshold loose and rely on the eye review in step 5 of §14.

14 · Execution order

Ordered so the two things that can kill the plan are tested in the first day, not the last. The 435k build must not be restarted or resumed.

#StepEffortKills the plan if
1Pilot Class F first — 10k plates from Flickr/Rawpixel via Openverse. Not Commons. This is the only class whose source is unproven, so it goes first. Eye-review the 10k.half a dayUnder 50% usable → cut F to 200k, and put background-removal on the app roadmap instead.
2Calibrate the relevance gate on one deep topic and one shallow one (sunset, coffee). Harvest to 10,000 each, score all, pick the cut by eye, measure the resulting keep rate.2 hNothing — but every number in §9 is a guess until this runs.
3Teach the crawler to harvest by search. generator=search + gsroffset + licence shard, replacing generator=allimages. Same prop=imageinfo, same iiurlwidth=384, same downstream. Frontier and cursor into the existing Qdrant checkpoint.half a dayNothing — the response shape is identical, verified.
4Crawl the Quality/Featured/Valued layer — 487k flat, licence-filtered, first. Live end-to-end test of the whole pipeline at real scale, and it seeds every class at once.~2 hNothing; this is the safe warm-up.
5Write the topic list to 800–1,200, grouped by class, with the §11 targets as spending caps.1 dayThis is the real bottleneck. Everything downstream is throughput.
6Pilot Class D and Class G at 25k each — the culturally specific one and the one I cut hardest. Eye-review both.3 hD under-delivers → the differentiation argument in §11 weakens and Class C should absorb the budget.
7Full build, 40 Pro-tier runners, claim queue over topics, --no-archive, per-host limits, class order A → C → D → B → E → F → G.21–30 h over ~5 runs—
8Harden: query-time near-duplicate cap, safety backfill over the legacy 435k, LOCAL_SPARSE=1 cutover, report/takedown endpoint, query logging.1–2 daysQuery logging is what replaces this entire document with data.

Why Class F goes first. final-report.html §9 also puts the weak pilots early, and it is right about the principle — pilot where failure lives. But it pilots textures on Commons, which I can already tell you fails (§7). Piloting the same bucket against the source that might actually serve it is the version of that step that can return new information.

15 · Serving, safety, duplicates, model, cost

Serving stays free, and now for every source

Commons: keep thumb_origin at iiurlwidth=384, served from thumb.wikimedia.org — 0 failures across 1,669 origins in TEST-DRIVE.md Step A, against 39% on upload.wikimedia.org. Never wsrv.nl. Flickr: store the _n (320px) URL derived by suffix substitution, 25.8 KB measured. Met: store primaryImageSmall, 38.7 KB measured. No bucket, no egress allowance, no card, for any source.

One contingency worth writing down rather than discovering: if Wikimedia ever objects to a commercial app driving sustained CDN traffic, the fallback is the already-scoped B2 path at 202 GB / ~$1.21 per month, and --no-embed plus embed_manifest.py still exist to build it.

Safety

Unchanged: score in-crawl, threshold 0.005, filter as must_not(safety >= SAFETY_MAX) so unscored legacy rows still pass. Two things this plan adds. First, search harvesting is safer than enumeration by construction — you never walk into a category you did not ask for. Second, the legacy 435k are still unscored and must be backfilled before 10M makes the ratio worse.

Duplicates

Measured at 1.5% within cosine 0.98 and 11.5% within 0.95, on a corpus built from curated topics — and the live "earth from space" row shows what that looks like to a user. Topic harvesting will make it worse, not better, because many topics retrieve the same famous images. Two cheap mitigations: dedupe by page id across topics at ingest (free), and cap per-cluster results in the top 20 at query time (one pass over rows already being returned).

Model

Upgrade to ViT-B-16-SigLIP2 / webli before the build, not after. Verified from the installed open_clip: embed_dim=768, image_size=224, context_length=64 — identical geometry, so the collection config, the padding-64 rule and the pad_id=1 fix all carry over untouched. Building 10M on the old model and upgrading later means re-crawling 10M.

One cost Gemini's recommendation misses. A model swap invalidates safety-prompts.npz and the 0.005 threshold. The frozen 28×768 matrix is in the old model's text space, and the logit scale and bias are per-model. Re-freeze the prompts and re-run testdrive/calibrate_safety.py as part of the swap — it is an afternoon, but skipping it silently disables the safety filter.

Cost

Crawl, embed, thumbnails and egress remain $0. The only recurring cost is the Hetzner box holding Qdrant and the API. Step D's winner stands: int8 on disk, always_ram: false, 95.2% recall@10, 10.7 ms p99, ~5 GB RAM and ~56 GB disk at 10M, on the CAX21 that is already running.

SigLIP 2's retrieval improvement on this corpus. The dimensional drop-in is verified; the quality gain is not.unverifiedRe-embed the 10-query recall set from TEST-DRIVE.md Step 0 with both models and compare top-10 ids.
The relevance gate's true keep rate, and therefore the 14.9M → 10M arithmetic in §9.estimatedStep 2 of §14 measures it directly in two hours.

Per-topic overlap rate across 800–1,200 topics.unknownFalls out of step 4 — the Quality-images layer will collide with everything, and the page-id dedup counter measures it for free.

In one paragraph

Keep the target at 10M and change three things about how it is built. Harvest by relevance search with a licence shard, not by walking category trees, because the ten-thousandth search result beats the fiftieth category member and 56% of an unsharded Commons crawl is invisible to a default user anyway. Keep Openverse, because the best rows in the running index are already 80% Openverse and Flickr serves its own 320px derivatives for free, so multi-source costs nothing and its absence costs the plates. And stop treating bucket sizes as targets: per-topic yield varies twenty-fold and is not predictable, so the artefact that determines the corpus is a list of 800–1,200 topics plus a relevance gate that decides how deep each one goes. The table in §11 is where to spend, in what order; the gate is what actually builds it.

Method. Every count in this document came from a live API call made on 10 September 2026 — commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php, api.openverse.org, collectionapi.metmuseum.org, live.staticflickr.com, and the project's own /api/search on the Hetzner box. The relevance experiment ran ViT-B-16-SigLIP / webli from this repo's venv on MPS with the model's own logit_scale=117.33, logit_bias=-12.93. Contact sheets are unretouched, in rank order, at the ranks stated. Demand figures are from Pexels' published popular-searches page and Unsplash's published Today page, read the same day.
